Firm guide · reviewed October 2026

Topstep challenge rules and how to pass the Combine

Topstep combines a trailing threshold with an explicit daily loss limit and a best-day consistency expectation. That is three constraints where most futures firms apply two, and it changes how an evaluation has to be paced. This guide covers each rule, the sizing that survives them, and the mistakes that end attempts.

Key takeaways

  • A best-day consistency expectation shapes the evaluation itself, not just the payout: your largest day should stay well under half the target.

The rules, laid out

ParameterHow it worksWhat it means in practice
Profit targetFixed dollar target per account sizeConvert to a percentage before comparing firms
Trailing thresholdFollows peak equity upwardProgress reduces room; size must fall near the end
Daily loss limitExplicit, resets each sessionThe tighter of the two limits governs the day
ConsistencyBest-day expectation applied to the evaluation and at payoutNo single session should dominate total profit
Minimum daysSet by the firm's current termsPace the target to arrive on or after the count

The distinctive feature of this rulebook is the overlap. Most futures firms rely on a trailing threshold and treat it as the daily constraint; Topstep states a daily loss limit separately. On a day when the trailing floor is far beneath current equity, the daily limit binds. On a day after a strong session — when the floor has risen close to equity — the trailing threshold binds first. A plan that models only one of the two will be wrong on roughly half of its sessions.

Two comparisons are worth having in mind before choosing a futures firm. Against Apex, the important difference is explicitness: Topstep's failure conditions are stated more plainly, which makes them easier to plan around once read properly. Against firms offering end-of-day trailing thresholds, Topstep's intraday behaviour is stricter — the floor moves on unrealised profit, not on closed profit, so an unrealised gain that retraces has already tightened the account.

Two loss rules at once

The trailing threshold is the rule traders underestimate, and the daily limit is the rule they misread. Both deserve precise treatment.

The trailing threshold

The failure level rises with your peak equity and never comes back down. Suppose a $100,000 account opens with a threshold $4,000 below the starting balance. If intraday equity reaches $104,000, the threshold rises with it, and a normal retracement to $101,500 leaves roughly $1,500 of room — on an account that is still up on the day.

The critical detail is that the threshold responds to unrealised equity on an intraday structure. A position $3,000 in the money has moved the floor even before anything is banked. When that position is closed at +$1,200 after a retracement, the floor stays where the peak pushed it. The trader banked less than the floor moved, and the cushion is permanently smaller.
